To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
calcium differentially alters behavioral sensitivity and Purkinje neuron electrophysiological sensitivity to ethanol in selectively inbred mice.

(1) Calcium differentially alters behavioral sensitivity to the hypnotic effects of ethanol in two selectively bred lines of mice, and (2) calcium differentially alters the electrophysiological sensitivity of Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum to the depressant effect of locally applied ethanol.
the calcium-dependent mechanisms are involved in behavioral and neurophysiological responses to ethanol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of calcium in ethanol intoxication and the possible role of calcium in genetically selected differences in ethanol sensitivity.
the genetic basis of ethanol sensitivity and the role of calcium in this sensitivity.
the role of calcium in ethanol intoxication.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
calcium differentially affects ethanol sensitivity in selectively bred mice, which may be related to differences in the electrophysiological response of Purkinje cells to ethanol.
calcium may be involved in ethanol intoxication and the effects of ethanol on cerebellar Purkinge neurons.
the effects of calcium in the central nervous system on the sensitivity to ethanol are complex and depend on the genetic background, the dose of ethanol and the dose of calcium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the calcium-dependent mechanism of ethanol intoxication is genetically controlled.
the calcium-dependent mechanisms are more important to the behavioral sensitivity to ethanol in SS mice than they are in LS mice.
the effects of ethanol on cerebellar Purkinge neurons are modulated by intracellular calcium levels and that the effects of alcohol are differentially regulated in selectively bred mouse populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is an important interaction between ethanol and calcium.
there is a genetic basis for ethanol’s effects on the brain, and this is likely to be important for understanding the genetic basis of addiction.
